### page_2
21 Abstract
22 Paleogeographic reconstructions based on paleomagnetic data rely on the reliability of
23 the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) as a primary geomagnetic signal.
24 Remagnetizations, however, can be common in many rock types, including late Paleozoic
25 and Mesozoic red beds, and they complicate paleogeographic interpretations. Extracting the
26 primary NRM from partially remagnetized rocks, and understanding the remagnetization
27 mechanism are important in these contexts. We carried out a systematic paleomagnetic study
28 of red bed samples from the Triassic Huangmaqing Formation, Nanjing (32.0°N, 118.9°E),
29 South China. Two NRM components carried by secondary and primary hematite are isolated
30 in 47 of the 94 samples studied, where the latter component has a direction in stratigraphic
31 coordinates of D = 29.2°, I = 34.6° ((cid:68) = 10.9°, 47 samples from 6 sites) that yields a
95
32 paleopole of λ = 60.8°N, ϕ = 228.1°E, dp/dm = 12.5/7.2, which is consistent with Triassic
33 pole positions for the South China Block. A secondary chemical remanent magnetization
34 (CRM) (D = 227.1°, I = 80.8°, (cid:68) = 7.3°) is documented in all 94 samples from 10 sites and
95
35 is carried by pigmentary hematite that is inferred to have been generated by magnetite
36 oxidation during orogenic activity. This secondary component has steep inclinations and is
37 interpreted to have been influenced by a combination of the remanence carried by original
38 parent magnetite, the orogenic stress field, and the prevailing geomagnetic field direction
39 during deformation. This CRM direction is recorded commonly by red beds from the South
40 China Block, and is significant for regional tectonic studies in the area.
41
42 Keywords: remagnetization, red beds, hematite, chemical remanent magnetization, detrital
43 remanent magnetization, South China Block, Triassic
44
2

### page_3
45 1. Introduction
46 Remagnetization, a phenomenon by which a natural remanent magnetization (NRM) is
47 acquired in an ambient magnetic field of a much younger age than that of the rock or
48 sediment itself, complicates interpretation of paleomagnetic data from rocks, soils, and
49 sediments (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Suk et al., 1993; Lu et al., 1994; Piper et al., 1999;
50 Roberts and Weaver, 2005; Rowan and Roberts, 2006; Deng et al., 2007; Jin and Liu, 2011;
51 Liu et al., 2011; van der Voo and Torsvik, 2012; Roberts, 2015). Generally,
52 remagnetization mechanisms involve several pathways, 1) mineral transformations
53 associated with redox process, i.e. magnetite, greigite, or pyrrhotite formation (Katz et
54 al., 2000; Weaver et al., 2002; Roberts and Weaver, 2005), 2) deformation-associated
55 fluid migration and/or pressure solution (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Elmore and
56 McCabe, 1991; Housen et al., 1993), 3) chemical weathering in moist, tropical
57 weathering, and soil-forming environments (Creer, 1961, 1968; Jin and Liu, 2011; Liu
58 et al., 2011), or 4) thermoviscous remanent magnetization acquisition (Scotese et al.,
59 1982; Kent, 1985; Hashimoto et al., 2008; Globokar, 2014). Acquisition of secondary
60 magnetizations through any such mechanism will obscure the primary paleomagnetic record
61 (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; van der Voo and Torsvik, 2012), and may lead to inaccurate
62 paleomagnetic interpretations if not recognized (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; van der Voo
63 and Torsvik, 2012; Dekkers, 2012).
64 In the South China Block (SCB), widely distributed late Paleozoic and Mesozoic red
65 beds have been subjected to extensive paleomagnetic investigations, aimed at reconstructing
66 regional paleogeography (e.g. Achache et al., 1984; Zaman and Torii, 1999; Steiner and
67 Lucas, 2000; Sun et al., 2006). However, the reliability of the NRM recorded by red
68 sediments is often questioned because widespread and largely pervasive remagnetizations
69 have been documented (Dobson and Heller, 1992; Wang and van der Voo, 1993; Huang and
3

### page_4
70 Opdyke, 1996; Liu et al., 2011). The prevalent remagnetization scenario is considered to be
71 some form of chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) acquired long after deposition
72 (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Elmore et al., 2012; van der Voo and Torsvik, 2012). The most
73 frequently occurring CRM carrier in red beds is hematite pigment, which can overprint a
74 detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) carried by primary hematite. Therefore,
75 discrimination of a CRM from a DRM is central to paleomagnetic studies of red beds.
76 Hematites from different environments have distinct morphologies, crystallinity ranges, and
77 magnetic properties (Collinson, 1965; Walker et al., 1981; Sugimoto et al., 1993, 1998;
78 Jiang et al., 2012, 2014), which can be used to distinguish the origin of the hematite under
79 investigation.
80 Thermal demagnetization (TD) is the most popular method for identifying a DRM or
81 CRM in red beds due to their different unblocking temperature spectra (McClelland-Brown,
82 1982; Iosifidi et al., 2010; Jiang et al., 2015). Detrital hematite has a narrow unblocking
83 temperature spectrum at the highest temperatures (~660-680 (cid:113)C) because it usually occurs as
84 stable single domain (SD) particles with often close to ideal stoichiometry. Pigmentary
85 hematite is typically finer-grained with sizes closer to the superparamagnetic (SP) to SD
86 threshold size, so that it has a much broader unblocking temperature spectrum at lower
87 temperatures (300-650 (cid:113)C) (Stokking and Tauxe, 1990a; Jiang et al., 2015). Alternating field
88 demagnetization (AFD) is also important in paleomagnetic studies, but it is not particularly
89 effective for treating red beds because hematite has high coercivities (Butler, 1992; Dunlop
90 and Özdemir, 1997). Chemical demagnetization (CD) has been used only occasionally for
91 analyzing red sediments with multiple NRM components within a single sample (Burek,
92 1969; Collinson, 1975; Kent and Opdyke, 1978; Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980; Tan et al.,
93 2007). Most rocks contain a relatively large number of remanence-carrying grains that have
94 variable chemical and physical properties. Ideally, the remanence in certain grains will be
4

### page_5
95 effectively removed by chemical dissolution during CD, whereas in others it will remain
96 unchanged. As the level of demagnetization (i.e. hematite dissolution) increases, the number
97 of grains affected also increases (Larson, 1981). Grains that are more likely to acquire
98 secondary magnetic components are more susceptible to lower levels of demagnetization.
99 The fine-grained hematite pigment will dissolve first, leaving behind partially dissolved
100 coarser specularite grains (Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980; Tan et al., 2007). This would
101 allow identification of the NRM component carried by detrital specularite.
102 For remagnetized red beds, it is difficult to isolate the characteristic remanent
103 magnetization (ChRM) and to establish it as the primary NRM component, especially in
104 pervasively remagnetized red beds. The relative effectiveness of the various
105 demagnetization techniques for identifying the advantages and disadvantages of each
106 method has yet to be tested widely for remagnetized red beds. Therefore, in this study, we
107 carried out systematic TD, CD, and combined CD-TD, with associated rock magnetic
108 analysis, on 94 remagnetized red bed samples to assess their efficacy for paleomagnetic
109 analysis of remagnetized red bed samples and to investigate the mechanisms by which
110 remagnetization occurred.
111
112 2. Sampling and measurements
113 2.1 Sampling
114 The Middle Triassic Huangmaqing Formation is investigated here. A total of 94
115 standard paleomagnetic cores (10 sites) with 25-mm diameter, were collected in a transect
116 from the village of Xiawuqi to Zijinshan Hill to the northeast of Nanjing, South China
117 (32.0(cid:113)N, 118.9(cid:113)E) (Figure 1a). The Huangmaqing Formation consists of clastic rocks,
118 including purplish-red siltstones and fine sandstones (Figure 1b). The beds dip shallowly to
119 the south (7-22(cid:113)). Paleomagnetic samples were cored with a portable drill and were oriented
5

### page_6
120 magnetically. Core samples were cut into three cylindrical sister-specimens 1-cm in length
121 in the laboratory for TD, combined CD-TD treatment on NRM, and combined CD-TD
122 treatment on three-orthogonal isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM) components
123 (Lowrie, 1990). Fresh off-cuts that remained after cutting specimens were used for other
124 rock magnetic measurements.
125
126 2.2 Paleomagnetic measurements
127 One set of sister-specimens (94 samples) was subjected to stepwise TD measurements
128 in 33 steps up to 695 (cid:113)C at 50 (cid:113)C intervals from 20 to 600 (cid:113)C and at 5 (cid:113)C intervals from 600
129 to 695 (cid:113)C using a thermal demagnetizer (PGL-100) developed at the Paleomagnetism and
130 Geochronology Laboratory (PGL), Institute of Geology and Geophysics, Chinese Academy
131 of Sciences, Beijing, China, in a magnetically shielded room. Remanent magnetizations
132 after each TD step were measured with a 2-G Enterprises RAPID three-axis magnetometer
133 (Kirschvink et al., 2008).
134 A second set of sister-specimens was subjected to combined CD-TD treatment. First,
135 specimens were subjected to chemical leaching experiments. To increase the surface area of
136 samples for more pervasive acid percolation, 0.5-mm diameter holes were drilled into each
137 side of the cylinders (Figure 1c). CD was carried out using 8 N (normality) hydrochloric
138 acid (HCl). Specimens from each site were soaked in a plastic bottle with 100 ml of acid.
139 The specimen bottles were placed in a magnetically shielded space, where the ambient field
140 was kept constant (<200 nT) within a set of Helmholtz coils. Initially, specimens were
141 measured magnetically after every three hours of leaching. Specimens were washed with
142 distilled water at each step, and were dried in a furnace at 40(cid:113)C in a magnetically shielded
143 space before measuring the remaining NRM to prevent the wet specimens and still slightly
144 acidic leachate from damaging the magnetometer. After each measurement the specimens
6

### page_7
145 were re-soaked in fresh acid (100 ml each time). After the first three steps, samples were
146 soaked in acid for 24 hours at each step. When the remanence became stable at ~20% of the
147 initial NRM on further demagnetization, the leaching process was considered complete.
148 Fourteen chemical leaching steps were performed, with three steps of 3-hour soakings and
149 eleven steps of 24-hour soakings. Afterward, the samples were subjected to a cycle of TD
150 measurements to remove the remaining NRM.
151
152 2.3 Rock magnetic measurements
153 To investigate the magnetic mineralogy, hysteresis loops for 40 representative samples
154 from all sites (4 samples from each site) were measured to a maximum field of 1 T using a
155 Princeton Measurements Corporation vibrating sample magnetometer (MicroMag VSM
156 3900), from which the coervicity (B ), saturation remanent magnetization (M), and
c r
157 saturation magnetization (M ) were determined. Isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM)
s
158 acquisition curves and back-field demagnetization curves were measured for the same
159 samples to determine the coercivity of remanence (B ). First derivatives of IRM acquisition
cr
160 curves were fitted with coercivity components following Kruiver et al. (2001) and Heslop et
161 al. (2002). For further magnetic mineralogy analyses, the temperature dependence of
162 magnetization (M-T) was measured in a steady 1 T field from room temperature to 800 °C
163 in air with a Magnetic Measurements variable field translation balance (VFTB). Zero-field
164 cooled (ZFC) warming curves were measured with a Quantum Design Magnetic Properties
165 Measurement System (MPMS XP-5, sensitivity 5.0(cid:117)10-10 Am2) for samples before and after
166 total CD treatment to detect changes in magnetic mineralogy. Samples were first cooled
167 from room temperature to 15 K in zero-field and were then exposed to a field of 5 T (this
168 IRM is denoted as IRM ). After the magnetic field was switched off, IRM was measured
5 T 5 T
169 from 15 to 300 K at 2.5 K intervals.
7

### page_8
170 A final set of sister specimens was used for stepwise CD-TD measurements of a
171 three-component IRM following the procedure of Lowrie (1990) to monitor the leaching
172 and thermal behaviour of the different coercivity components. First, samples were
173 magnetized in successively smaller fields along three mutually perpendicular sample axes
174 (2.5 T along the z-axis, 0.5 T along the y-axis, and 0.05 T along the x-axis, respectively).
175 The samples were then subjected to CD-TD measurements following the same procedure as
176 for the second group of sister-specimens in the NRM demagnetization process.
177 To measure magnetic property variations during CD, fresh offcut samples were also
178 subjected to 14 steps of stepwise chemical leaching in the same batch as the oriented
179 samples for NRM demagnetization. Hysteresis loops and IRM acquisition curves were
180 measured after each leaching step. This is the first study in which rock magnetic properties
181 of red beds have been monitored during chemical leaching.
182
183 3. Results
184 3.1 Paleo- and rock magnetic characterization of red bed samples
185 Typical NRM intensities for the studied specimens are about 10-2 A/m. Based on TD
186 results, samples can be divided into three groups. Samples from individual sites have similar
187 demagnetization behaviour, i.e. most samples are allocated to the same group. Group I
188 samples (~39 specimens/4 sites) have relatively straightforward demagnetization behaviour
189 characterized by a single linear trajectory between 100 and 660 (cid:113)C (Figure 2a-1). This
190 indicates that hematite is a significant ChRM carrier. The magnetization direction is oriented
191 to the northwest with moderate to steep-downward-directed inclinations in in-situ
192 coordinates. Directions for each site before and after tilt correction are summarized in Table
193 1. They differ from the present-day geomagnetic field direction before bedding correction.
194 M-T curves decrease gradually during heating and reach zero at ~670 (cid:113)C, which further
8

### page_9
195 indicates that hematite is the dominant magnetic mineral (Figure 2a-4). A bulk coercivity B
c
196 of 342 mT was determined from the hysteresis loop after slope correction between 0.9
197 and 1 T (Figure 2a-2). This B value should be considered as a lower bound since it is
c
198 based on a minor hysteresis loop: the maximum available applied field of 1 T is
199 insufficient to saturate the samples at room temperature magnetically. However, IRM
200 component analysis indicates that two coercivity components can be identified, a dominant
201 component with median acquisition field (B ) of 600-630 mT that contributes 90% of the
H1/2
202 IRM and a small component (10%) with median acquisition field (B ) of ~100 mT (Figure
L1/2
203 2a-3).
204 In Group II samples (~14 specimens/2 sites), two NRM components are identified from
205 TD analysis (Figure 2b-1). Component A (Comp A) is isolated below 670 (cid:113)C, and accounts
206 for 70-80% of the initial NRM intensity. It is northwest-directed with a steep positive
207 inclination, close to the direction of Group I samples, which is distinct from the present-day
208 geomagnetic field direction. A second component, designated as component B (Comp B), is
209 resolved between 670 and 690 (cid:113)C with 5 demagnetization steps and is directed to the
210 northwest with a shallow negative inclination in geographic coordinates. M-T curves decay
211 gradually to 670 (cid:113)C and then drop to zero abruptly at ~685 (cid:113)C, which is consistent with the
212 NRM TD results (Figure 2b-4). Bulk B for a representative sample is ~398 mT, again a
c
213 lower bound value derived from an unsaturated hysteresis loop (Figure 2b-2), with two
214 coercivity components identified from IRM analysis with B of 700-710 mT (i.e. higher
H1/2
215 than that of Group I) and B of ~200 mT (Figure 2b-3) (higher than that of Group I).
L1/2
216 Group III samples (~33 specimens/4 sites) also have two magnetic components, where
217 Comp A dominates up to 670 (cid:113)C with a northeast direction and steep downward-directed
218 inclination in situ, and Comp B (based on 5 demagnetization levels) is resolved from 670
219 to 690 (cid:113)C with a northeast direction and shallow positive inclination (Figure 2c-1). M-T
9

### page_10
220 curves of Group III samples are similar to those of Group II samples, with magnetic
221 ordering temperatures of ~685 (cid:113)C (Figure 2c-4). The bulk B for representative Group III
c
222 samples is ~230 mT (Figure 2c-2), and IRM acquisition curves can be fitted with two
223 components with B of ~430 mT and B of ~60-65 mT (Figure 2c-3), both lower than
H1/2 L1/2
224 the equivalent fractions in Groups I and II.
225 The model of Jiang et al. (2015) was used to analyze NRM TD curves for the three
226 sample groups to assess whether the NRM is a CRM or a DRM. This model was developed
227 mainly for red bed samples, and discriminates between two types of hematite, specular
228 grains and red pigment, which are known to occur in red beds. The former have
229 coarser grain sizes and record a DRM and fine-grained pigment records a CRM.
230 Blocking temperature is related positively to particle size in the stable SD state based
231 on Néel theory (Dunlop and Özdemir, 1997), hence the maximum unblocking
232 temperature of DRM is higher than that of CRM. Also, based on the results of Jiang et
233 al. (2015) and references therein, DRM and CRM decay curves have different shapes.
234 Therefore, these distinct differences may be used to distinguish CRM from (most of the)
235 DRM in red beds. Although the unblocking temperature spectra of CRM recorded by
236 coarse particles will overlap with that of DRM and complicate their distinction as
237 NRM components, this method can be useful as a secondary, supporting line of
238 evidence to discriminate CRM and DRM in red beds. Curves for Group I samples have a
239 concave shape and decay to zero gradually, which is consistent with expected CRM
240 behaviour (Figure 3a). Samples from the other two groups have curves with similar shapes
241 to those expected for a DRM, with abrupt decreases to zero at ~670-690 (cid:113)C (Figure 3b).
242 Based on TD and rock magnetic results, Group I samples are interpreted to have been
243 completely remagnetized by a CRM, while samples from the other two groups are partially
244 remagnetized and record a mixture of a CRM and a DRM.
10

### page_11
245
246 3.2 Rock magnetic monitoring of CD-TD behaviour of red bed samples
247 To monitor the CD-TD behaviour of different coercivity components, stepwise CD-TD
248 treatment of a three-component IRM was carried out on a series of sister specimens. Before
249 CD treatment, the medium (50-500 mT) and hard (>500 mT) components are dominant
250 (Figure 4a-c). During stepwise CD treatment, the IRM decreases sharply to become constant
251 after six steps for Group I samples (Figure 4a), while for the other two sample groups, the
252 IRM is more resistant to CD treatment and ceases to decrease further after 12 and 8 steps,
253 respectively (Figure 4b, c). During subsequent TD treatment, the medium coercivity
254 component is dominant. The soft component for all samples is unblocked below ~600 (cid:113)C,
255 while the medium and hard components are completely unblocked at ~680 (cid:113)C. In addition, a
256 weak Verwey transition is detected in low-temperature ZFC curves (Figure 5a-c), which
257 indicates that magnetite occurs in the samples. For samples after 14-step CD treatment, an
258 obvious Verwey transition is observed but the IRM intensity has decreased to 10% of that
259 before CD treatment (Figure 5d-f). We infer that the expression due to magnetite may be
260 concealed by massive amounts of hematite in the non-leached samples. After CD treatment,
261 hematite pigment is dissolved, so magnetite can be detected more easily with magnetic
262 methods, which supports the notion that pigmentary hematite is dissolved preferentially, and
263 that detrital magnetite is more difficult to dissolve (Hu et al., 2013). Therefore, we conclude
264 that magnetite is responsible for the soft IRM component and that hematite is responsible
265 for the latter two components.
266 IRM acquisition curves after each CD leaching step were determined for 52 samples.
267 Two coercivity components can be identified from the IRM acquisition curves, a dominant
268 component with high coercivity of B and a soft component with coercivity of B
H1/2 L1/2
269 (representative examples are shown in Figure 4d-f and Table 2). B and B decrease
H1/2 L1/2
11

### page_12
270 during progressive CD treatment for samples from the three identified groups. For Group I
271 samples (13 specimens), B decreases from ~800 mT to ~100 mT, while B decreases
H1/2 L1/2
272 from ~80 mT to ~20 mT (Figure 4d), which leads to a decreasing bulk B . It also suggests
cr
273 that both the “hard” and “soft” components are attacked by the acid, so that coarse and fine
274 particles become finer or are dissolved completely. For sample groups II and III, coercivity
275 variations during CD treatment are not as marked as for Group I samples (Figure 4d-f). For
276 Group II samples (6 specimens), B decreases from ~700 to ~400 mT, and B decreases
H1/2 L1/2
277 from ~200 to ~40 mT (Figure 4e), while for Group III samples (33 specimens), B
H1/2
278 decreases from ~500 to ~200 mT, and B decreases from ~60 to ~20 mT (Figure 4f).
L1/2
279 Based on the three-component IRM features (Figure 4a-c) and low temperature results
280 (Figure 5), the low coercivity component with B around 20 mT is interpreted to be
L1/2
281 magnetite.
282
283 3.3 Comparison of chemical and thermal demagnetization results
284 For Group I samples, the primary NRM is difficult to identify with TD because it is
285 overprinted completely by a secondary CRM. However, a potentially meaningful ChRM
286 component can be identified from TD results for Groups II and III. Group I samples have a
287 brighter red colour and seem to be more pigmented than the others which could explain the
288 absence of a primary ChRM. This raises the question of whether CD is more effective in
289 isolating a ChRM in red beds, and whether it can resolve a ChRM for Group I.
290 TD only (referred to as ‘direct TD’), CD, and combined CD-TD results are summarized
291 in Figure 6. Group I samples have a single linear trajectory in both CD and TD; TD applied
292 after completion of CD also reveals the same trajectory (Figure 6a). In equal-area
293 projections, demagnetization trajectories for TD and CD-TD overlap (Figure 6b). For
294 stepwise CD and TD, about half of the NRM was demagnetized by CD (Figure 6c), with CD
12

### page_13
295 causing bleaching of the initially red samples (Figure 1c, d). For Group II samples, direct
296 TD and combined CD-TD yield contrasting results. A primary reversed polarity direction
297 was extracted from direct TD, while for the stepwise CD-TD protocol, two components are
298 identified. One component is similar to Comp A identified in the direct TD protocol, while
299 the direction for the latter is almost a vector combination of the two components extracted
300 from direct TD measurements (Figure 6d, e). Only 10% of the NRM is left after CD (Figure
301 6f). For Group III samples, CD-TD reveals two components, which are essentially parallel
302 to the two components identified from direct TD treatment (Figure 6g), with almost 85% of
303 the NRM removed by CD.
304
305 4. Discussion
306 4.1 Comparison of the effectiveness of thermal and chemical demagnetization
307 TD results allow identification of two components (Comps A and B) in samples from
308 Groups II and III (6 sites), while only Comp A can be distinguished in samples from Group I
309 (4 sites). Site mean directions (Fisher, 1953) are presented in Figure 7 and Table 1. The
310 formation site-averaged direction for Comp A for all three groups is D = 355.1(cid:113), I = 80.5(cid:113)
311 (N= 10, (cid:78) = 35.9, (cid:68) = 7.3°) (Figure 7a). Directions for Comp B fall into two groups, one
95
312 with positive inclinations with a formation mean direction of D/I = 29.3(cid:113)/16.8(cid:113) (N = 4, (cid:78) =
313 35.7,(cid:68) = 10.9°), and the other with negative inclinations (D/I = 229.9(cid:113)/-12.8(cid:113), N = 2, (cid:78) =
95
314 45, (cid:68) = 10.1°), which is consistent with previous results from this area (Opdyke et al.,
95
315 1986; Su et al., 2005) (Figure 7b). Comp B directions pass a reversals test at the 95%
316 significance level (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990). Although we cannot conduct a fold
317 test because the sampled Huangmaqing Formation red beds are monoclinal, the tilt test
318 (Watson and Enkin, 1993; Enkin, 2003) for Comp B gives a maximum grouping of
319 directions at 144 percent untilting (Figure S1). All of these observations indicate that Comp
13

### page_14
320 B has a pre-folding origin. Thus, thermal demagnetization is effective for analyzing partially
321 remagnetized red beds with dispersed unblocking temperature spectra. The direction
322 obtained from CD treatment is similar to that identified from TD for Comp A with steep
323 downward-directed inclinations (Figure 7c); however, Comp B cannot be isolated from
324 combined CD-TD treatment (Figure 7d). Our results indicate that TD is more effective than
325 CD, which raises the question of why CD is less effective in these samples.
326 Red bed NRMs are generally a composite of a DRM and CRM, where the former is
327 often thought to be carried by relatively coarse detrital magnetic minerals (i.e. hematite or
328 magnetite), while the latter is recorded by fine-grained hematite pigment (e.g. Collinson,
329 1974; Larson and Walker, 1975; McClelland, 1996; Iosifidi et al., 2010). Fine-grained
330 hematite pigment is expected to be more soluble than coarser detrital hematite particles. HCl
331 leaches all iron oxides, and removes the most soluble grains first leaving less soluble grains
332 behind (Burek, 1969; Park, 1970; Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980). For example,
333 fine-grained hematite cement has a propensity to dissolve and, therefore, dissolves readily,
334 leaving behind partially dissolved specularite (Henry, 1979; Cornell and Giovanoli, 1993).
335 This allows identification of the magnetization component carried by detrital specularite.
336 Therefore, CD could be useful when dealing with sediments with multicomponent
337 magnetizations within a single sample, such as a DRM and CRM. However, if the solubility
338 spectra of hematite cement and specularite overlap in some unknown fashion, simple vector
339 subtraction cannot be used to identify the respective components.
340 IRM unmixing analysis indicates that low- (~100-200 mT) and high-coercivity
341 (~500-700 mT) components can be separated (Figure 2), which may reflect different particle
342 size distributions of hematite based on the positive relationship of particle size and
343 coercivity. During acid leaching, the coercivities of the two components decrease
344 simultaneously (Figure 4e-f), which indicates a particle size decrease for both components
14

### page_15
345 (Hartstra, 1982; Dekkers and Linssen, 1989). Thus, fine and coarse particles both dissolve
346 during this process, so that the paleomagnetic direction identified with CD is in principle the
347 vector sum of the two components identified from direct TD (Figure 6d, g). Tauxe et al.
348 (1980) conducted chemical leaching on Siwalik red beds in which the dominant magnetic
349 carrier is hematite and found that the bulk remanent coercivity decreases after acid leaching,
350 so they deduced that hematite pigment is magnetically harder than specularite because they
351 assumed that only pigment was dissolved. Our results provide a reasonable explanation for
352 the decreased bulk coercivity, where both low and high coercivity components dissolve
353 during acid leaching (Figure 4d-f). Hematite is presumably present in various forms with
354 diverse origins (Walker et al., 1981), which refines the commonly held view that hematite in
355 red beds can be divided into just two groups: pigment and detrital specularite. Authigenic
356 hematite occurs not only as pigment, but also as microcrystalline, polycrystalline, and
357 monocrystalline grains with sizes in the micrometer range (Walker et al., 1981), which will
358 not dissolve as readily as pigment. Therefore, CD is not so effective in removing secondary
359 hematite with a wide particle size distribution. However, for red bed samples with distinct
360 particle size distributions, such as pigment and specularite, CD could provide meaningful
361 results (Henry, 1979; Tan et al., 2007).
362
363 4.2 Remagnetization mechanism for the steep magnetization component
364 A strong secondary vertically-directed magnetization component is often observed in
365 Triassic samples from South China (Figure 8), including the studied Huangmaqing
366 Formation in Nanjing (Kent et al., 1986, 1987; Opdyke et al., 1986; Su et al., 2005), the
367 Anshun and Huaxi Formations in Guizhou province (Huang and Opdyke, 1996, 2015) and
368 Hubei province (Huang and Opdyke, 1997, 2000), the Badong Formation in the border area
369 between Sichuan, Hubei, and Hunan provinces (Huang and Opdyke, 1991, 1992), and the
15

### page_16
370 Tongtoujian Formation in Anhui province (Gilder et al., 1999; Su et al., 2005). However, the
371 origin of this component is unclear (Opdyke et al., 1986). Previous studies have proposed
372 that it might represent a multicomponent magnetization that yields a vertical resultant, with
373 overprinting in a post-folding steeply inclined magnetic field (Opdyke et al., 1986) that
374 might be related to late Mesozoic Yanshanian orogenic activity in these parts of South China
375 (Kent et al., 1987; Wang and van der Voo, 1993), which led to substantial intracontinental
376 tectonic rotations.
377 Red bed remagnetization usually results from secondary hematite formation via
378 crystallization from solution or by mineral alteration. For the former mechanism, the CRM
379 can record faithfully the magnetic field direction if it is a single-stage growth process
380 (Stokking and Tauxe, 1987, 1990a; Jiang et al., 2015), while the magnetization direction for
381 the latter mechanism will be controlled by both the remanence of the parent mineral(s) and
382 the ambient magnetic field direction (Heider and Dunlop, 1987; Stokking and Tauxe, 1990b;
383 Madsen et al., 2002). In our experiments, only hematite components with unblocking
384 temperatures between ~650(cid:113)C and 685(cid:113)C are interpreted as a ChRM in the direct TD results
385 (Figure 2). However, based on CD-TD treatment of a three-component IRM, magnetite is
386 detected in the low-coercivity component with a Curie temperature below 600 (cid:113)C after CD
387 (Figure 4a-c); this component is not observed in direct TD results for a three-component
388 IRM because hematite is so dominant (Su et al., 2005). A Verwey transition is also more
389 evident in low-temperature ZFC curves for samples after CD treatment (Figure 5). We
390 deduce that this magnetite is concealed by its small concentration with respect to the large
391 hematite pigment concentration, which precludes its detection by direct TD. Magnetite may
392 also be a parent mineral for secondary hematite.
393 Paleomagnetic poles of Comp B (Figure 9) cluster alongside hematite-based poles
394 from previous studies with DRM unblocking between 670 and 690 °C and close to the
16

### page_17
395 position of Triassic paleomagnetic poles for the South China Block, which further
396 indicates that Comp B is a primary NRM component. However, the paleomagnetic pole
397 for Comp A lies far from the apparent polar wander path of the South China Block (Figure
398 9), which suggests that the recording of Comp A was controlled not only by the ambient
399 paleomagnetic field, but also by additional factors. Parent magnetic particles can control
400 second-generation particles through magnetostatic or exchange interactions (Stokking and
401 Tauxe, 1990b), which leads to a CRM with a direction intermediate between the ambient
402 magnetic field direction and the parent magnetic mineral direction (Heider and Dunlop,
403 1987; Stokking and Tauxe, 1990b). Late Mesozoic Yanshanian orogenic activity occurred
404 pervasively in the South China Block. Previous studies indicate that the studied Zijinshan
405 hill formed during the Yanshanian orogeny (Xue et al., 1985; Ge, 1987); the fluids produced
406 could have caused conditions required for magnetite oxidation (Kent et al., 1987). In
407 addition, the stress field of an orogeny can play a role in CRM acquisition by deviating it
408 from the ambient field direction (Nagata, 1970; Gilder, 2007). Therefore, we suggest that
409 the direction of the secondary component was controlled by several factors. Before the
410 orogenic activity and diagenesis, the paleomagnetic field is inferred to have been recorded
411 faithfully by Comp B, which is carried by detrital magnetite and hematite. However, during
412 or after tectonic activity, magnetite oxidation would have been promoted by the
413 accompanying temperature increase, and could have been accomplished by fluid flow
414 or by pressure solution (Housen et al., 1993). During this process, a tectonically rotated
415 parent remanence carried by magnetite with the influence of a contemporaneous ambient
416 geomagnetic field and stress field generated by tectonic activity are argued to have produced
417 the steep downward-directed magnetization in the studied samples. We suggest that this is
418 why a steep magnetization component is commonly observed in different areas of the South
419 China Block.
17

### page_18
420
421 5. Conclusions
422 Based on systematic thermal and chemical demagnetization, and rock magnetic
423 analysis, thermal demagnetization is shown to be more effective in isolating an apparently
424 primary magnetization than chemical demagnetization in red beds from South China. Two
425 remanence components carried by secondary and primary hematite are isolated with thermal
426 demagnetization, where the latter records a paleomagnetic direction that is consistent with
427 published results. However, chemical demagnetization fails to extract a ChRM direction
428 from the remagnetized component due to simultaneous dissolution of both fine and coarser
429 hematite particles.
430 The presence of magnetite provides clues to the remagnetization mechanism in these
431 samples. The CRM carried by secondary hematite is interpreted to have been generated by
432 magnetite oxidation during tectonic activity. Therefore, the secondary magnetization with
433 steep inclination, which is observed commonly in Triassic samples from different areas of
434 the South China Block, is interpreted to have been influenced by a combination of the
435 remanence carried by parent magnetite, the orogenic stress field, and the contemporaneous
436 geomagnetic field direction during deformation. Our results shed new light on interpretation
437 of paleomagnetic results from remagnetized red beds and are significant for tectonic studies
438 of southern China.

1

### page_33
21 Abstract
22 Paleogeographic reconstructions based on paleomagnetic data rely on the reliability
23 of the natural remanent magnetization (NRM) being primary. Remagnetizations can be
24 common in many rock types, including late Paleozoic and Mesozoic red beds, and they
25 complicate paleogeographic interpretations. Extracting the primary NRM from partially
26 remagnetized rocks, and understanding the remagnetization mechanism are important in
27 these contexts. We carried out a systematic paleomagnetic study of red bed samples from
28 the Triassic Huangmaqing Formation, Nanjing (32.0°N, 118.9°E), South China. Two
29 NRM components carried by secondary and primary hematite are isolated in 47 of the 94
30 samples studied, where the latter component has a direction in stratigraphic coordinates
31 of D = 29.2°, I = 34.6° ((cid:68) = 10.9°, 47 samples from 6 sites) that yield a paleopole of λ
95
32 =60.8°N, ϕ = 228.1°E, dp/dm = 12.5/7.2, which is consistent with Triassic pole positions
33 for the South China Block. A secondary chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) (D =
34 227.1°, I = 80.8°, (cid:68) = 7.3°) is documented in all 94 samples from 10 sites and is carried
95
35 by pigmentary hematite that is inferred to have been generated by magnetite oxidation
36 during orogenic activity. This secondary component has steep inclinations and is
37 interpreted to be influenced by a combination of the remanence carried by original parent
38 magnetite, the orogenic stress field, and the prevailing geomagnetic field direction during
39 deformation. This CRM direction is recorded commonly by red beds from the South
40 China Block, and is significant for regional tectonic studies in the area.
41
42 Keywords: remagnetization, red beds, hematite, chemical remanent magnetization,
43 detrital remanent magnetization, South China Block, Triassic
44
2

### page_34
45 1. Introduction
46 Remagnetization, a phenomenon by which the natural remanent magnetization
47 (NRM) is acquired in an ambient magnetic field of a much younger age than that of the
48 rock or sediment itself, complicates interpretation of paleomagnetic data from rocks, soils,
49 and sediments (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Suk et al., 1993; Lu et al., 1994; Piper et al.,
50 1999; Roberts and Weaver, 2005; Rowan and Roberts, 2006;Deng et al., 2007; Jin and
51 Liu, 2011; Liu et al., 2011; van der Voo and Torsvik, 2012; Roberts, 2015). Generally, the
52 mechanisms by which remagnetizations occur involve mineral transformations during
53 diagenesis, i.e. magnetite, greigite, or pyrrhotite formation (Katz et al., 2000; Weaver et
54 al., 2002; Roberts and Weaver, 2005), chemical weathering in moist, tropical weathering
55 and soil-forming environments (Creer, 1961, 1968; Jin and Liu, 2011; Liu et al., 2011), or
56 the acquisition of thermoviscous remanent magnetization (Scotese et al., 1982; Kent,
57 1985; Hashimoto et al., 2008; Globokar, 2014). Acquisition of secondary magnetizations
58 through any such mechanism will obscure the primary paleomagnetic record (McCabe
59 and Elmore, 1989; van der Voo and Torsvik, 2012), and may lead to inaccurate
60 paleomagnetic interpretations if not recognized (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; van der Voo
61 and Torsvik, 2012; Dekkers, 2012).
62 In the South China Block (SCB), widely distributed late Paleozoic and Mesozoic red
63 beds have been subjected to extensive paleomagnetic investigations, aimed at
64 reconstructing its paleogeography (e.g. Achache et al., 1984; Zaman and Torii, 1999;
65 Steiner and Lucas, 2000; Sun et al., 2006). However, the reliability of the NRM recorded
66 by red sediments is often questioned because widespread and often pervasive
67 remagnetizations have been documented (Dobson and Heller, 1992; Wang and van der
68 Voo, 1993; Huang and Opdyke, 1996; Liu et al., 2011). The prevalent remagnetization
69 scenario is considered to be some form of chemical remanent magnetization (CRM)
3

### page_35
70 acquired long after deposition (McCabe and Elmore, 1989; Elmore et al., 2012; van der
71 Voo and Torsvik, 2012). The most frequently occurring CRM carrier in red beds is
72 hematite pigment, which can overprint a detrital remanent magnetization (DRM) carried
73 by primary hematite. Therefore, discrimination of a CRM from a DRM is central to
74 paleomagnetic studies of red beds. Hematites from different environments have distinct
75 morphologies, crystallinity ranges, and magnetic properties (Collinson, 1965; Walker et
76 al., 1981; Sugimoto et al., 1993, 1998; Jiang et al., 2012, 2014), which can be used to
77 distinguish the origin of the hematite under investigation.
78 Thermal demagnetization (TD) is the most popular method for identifying a DRM
79 or CRM in red beds due to their different unblocking temperature spectra
80 (McClelland-Brown, 1982; Iosifidietal., 2010; Jiang et al., 2015). Detrital hematite has a
81 narrow unblocking temperature spectrum at the highest temperatures (~660-680 (cid:113)C)
82 because it usually occurs as stable single domain (SD) particles with often close to ideal
83 stoichiometry. Pigmentary hematite is typically finer-grained with sizes closer to the
84 superparamagnetic (SP) to SD threshold size, so that it has a much broader unblocking
85 temperature spectrum at lower temperatures (300-650 (cid:113)C) (Stokking and Tauxe, 1990a;
86 Jiang et al., 2015). Alternating field demagnetization (AFD) is also important in
87 paleomagnetic studies, but it is not particularly effective for treating red beds because
88 hematite has high coercivities (Butler, 1992; Dunlop and Özdemir, 1997). Chemical
89 demagnetization (CD) has been used only occasionally for analysing red sediments
90 with multiple NRM components within a single sample (Burek, 1969; Collinson, 1975;
91 Kent and Opdyke, 1978; Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980; Tan et al., 2007). Most rocks
92 contain a relatively large number of remanence-carrying grains that have variable
93 chemical and physical properties. Ideally, the remanence in certain grains will be
94 effectively removed by chemical dissolution during CD, whereas in others it will remain
4

### page_36
95 unchanged. As the level of demagnetization (i.e. hematite dissolution) increases, the
96 number of grains affected also increases (Larson, 1981). Grains that are more likely to
97 acquire secondary magnetic components are more susceptible to lower levels of
98 demagnetization. The fine-grained hematite pigment will dissolve first, leaving behind
99 partially dissolved coarser specularite grains (Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980; Tan et al.,
100 2007). This would allow identification of the NRM component carried by detrital
101 specularite.
102 For remagnetized red beds, it is difficult to isolate the characteristic remanent
103 magnetization (ChRM) and establish it as the primary NRM component, especially in
104 pervasively remagnetized red beds. The relative effectiveness of the various
105 demagnetization techniques to identify the advantages and disadvantages of each method
106 has yet to be tested widely for remagnetized red beds. Therefore, in this study, we carried
107 out systematic TD, CD, and combined CD-TD, with associated rock magnetic analysis,
108 on 94 remagnetized red bed samples to assess their efficacy for paleomagnetic analysis of
109 remagnetized red bed samples and to investigate the mechanisms by which
110 remagnetization occurred.
111
112 2. Sampling and measurements
113 2.1 Sampling
114 The Middle Triassic Huangmaqing Formation is investigated here. A total of 94
115 standard paleomagnetic cores (10 sites) with 25-mm diameter, were collected in a
116 transect from the village of Xiawuqi to Zijinshan Hill to the northeast of Nanjing, South
117 China (32.0(cid:113)N, 118.9(cid:113)E) (Figure 1a). The Huangmaqing Formation consists of clastic
118 rocks, including purplish-red siltstones and fine sandstones (Figure 1b). The beds dip
119 shallowly to the south (7-22(cid:113)). Paleomagnetic samples were cored with a portable drill
5

### page_37
120 and were oriented magnetically. Core samples were cut into three cylindrical
121 sister-specimens 1-cm in length in the laboratory for TD, combined CD-TD treatment on
122 NRM, and combined CD-TD treatment on three-orthogonal isothermal remanent
123 magnetization (IRM) components (Lowrie, 1990). Fresh off-cuts that remained after
124 cutting specimens were used for other rock magnetic measurements.
125
126 2.2 Paleomagnetic measurements
127 One set of sister-specimens (94 samples) was subjected to stepwise TD
128 measurements in 33 steps up to 695 (cid:113)C at 50 (cid:113)C intervals from 20 to 600 (cid:113)C and at 5 (cid:113)C
129 intervals from 600 to 695 (cid:113)C using a thermal demagnetizer (PGL-100) developed at the
130 Paleomagnetism and Geochronology Laboratory (PGL), Institute of Geology and
131 Geophysics, Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing, China in a magnetically shielded
132 room. Remanent magnetizations after each TD step were measured with a 2-G
133 Enterprises RAPID three-axis magnetometer (Kirschvink et al., 2008).
134 A second set of sister-specimens was subjected to combined CD-TD treatment. First,
135 specimens were subjected to chemical leaching experiments. To increase the surface area
136 of samples for more pervasive acid percolation, 0.5-mm diameter holes were drilled into
137 each side of the cylinders (Figure 1c). CD was carried out using 8 N (normality)
138 hydrochloric acid (HCl). Specimens from each site were soaked in a plastic bottle with
139 100 ml of acid. The specimen bottles were placed in a magnetically shielded space,
140 where the ambient field was kept constant (<200 nT) within a set of Helmholtz coils.
141 Initially, specimens were measured magnetically after every three hours of leaching.
142 Specimens were washed with distilled water at each step, and were dried in a furnace at
143 40(cid:113)C in a magnetically shielded space before measuring the remaining NRM to prevent
144 the wet specimens and still slightly acidic leachate from damaging the magnetometer.
6

### page_38
145 After each measurement the specimens were re-soaked in fresh acid (100 ml each time).
146 After the first three steps, samples were soaked in acid for 24 hours at each step. When
147 the remanence became stable at ~20% of the initial NRM on further demagnetization, the
148 leaching process was considered complete. Fourteen chemical leaching steps were
149 performed, with three steps of 3-hour soakings and eleven steps of 24 hour soakings.
150 Afterwards, the samples were subjected to a cycle of TD measurements to remove the
151 remaining NRM.
152
153 2.3 Rock magnetic measurements
154 To investigate the magnetic mineralogy, hysteresis loops for 40 representative
155 samples from all sites (4 samples from each site) were measured to a maximum field of 1
156 T using a Princeton Measurements Corporation vibrating sample magnetometer
157 (MicroMagVSM 3900), from which the coervicity (B ), saturation remanent
c
158 magnetization (M), and saturation magnetization (M ) were determined. Isothermal
r s
159 remanent magnetization (IRM) acquisition curves and back-field demagnetization curves
160 were measured for the same samples to determine the coercivity of remanence (B ). First
cr
161 derivatives of IRM acquisition curves were fitted with coercivity components following
162 Kruiver et al. (2001) and Heslop et al. (2002). For further magnetic mineralogy analyses,
163 the temperature dependence of magnetization (M-T) was measured in a steady 1 T field
164 from room temperature to 800°C in air with a Magnetic Measurements variable field
165 translation balance (VFTB). Zero-field cooled (ZFC) warming curves were measured
166 with a Quantum Design Magnetic Properties Measurement System (MPMS XP-5,
167 sensitivity 5.0(cid:117)10-10 Am2) for samples before and after total CD treatment to detect
168 changes in magnetic mineralogy. Samples were first cooled from room temperature to 15
169 K in zero field and were then exposed to a field of 5 T (this IRM is denoted as IRM ).
5 T
7

### page_39
170 After the magnetic field was switched off, IRM was measured from 15 to 300 K at 2.5
5 T
171 K intervals.
172 A final set of sister specimens was used for stepwise CD-TD measurements of a
173 three-component IRM following the procedure of Lowrie (1990) to monitor the leaching
174 and thermal behaviour of the different coercivity components. First, samples were
175 magnetized in successively smaller fields along three mutually perpendicular sample axes
176 (2.5 T along the z-axis, 0.5 T along the y-axis, and 0.05 T along the x-axis, respectively).
177 The samples were then subjected to CD-TD measurements following the same procedure
178 as for the second group of sister-specimens in the NRM demagnetization process.
179 To measure magnetic property variations during CD, fresh offcut samples were also
180 subjected to 14 steps of stepwise chemical leaching in the same batch as the oriented
181 samples for NRM demagnetization. Hysteresis loops and IRM acquisition curves were
182 measured after each leaching step. This is the first study in which rock magnetic
183 properties of red beds have been monitored during chemical leaching.
184
185 3. Results
186 3.1 Paleo- and rock magnetic characterization of red bed samples
187 Typical NRM intensities for the studied specimens are about 10-2 A/m. Based on TD
188 results, samples can be divided into three groups. Samples from individual sites have
189 similar demagnetization behaviour, i.e. most samples are allocated to the same group.
190 Group I samples (~39 specimens / 4 sites) have relatively straightforward
191 demagnetization behaviour characterized by a single linear trajectory between 100 and
192 660 (cid:113)C (Figure 2a-1). This indicates that hematite is a significant ChRM carrier. The
193 magnetization direction is oriented to the northwest with moderate to
194 steep-downward-directed inclinations in in-situ coordinates. Directions for each site
8

### page_40
195 before and after tilt correction are summarized in Table 1. They differ from the
196 present-day geomagnetic field direction before bedding correction. M-T curves decrease
197 gradually during heating and reach zero at ~670 (cid:113)C, which further indicates that hematite
198 is the dominant magnetic mineral (Figure 2a-4). A maximum applied field of 1 T was
199 insufficient to magnetically saturate the samples at room temperature, with a bulk
200 coercivity B of 342 mT determined from the hysteresis loop after slope correction
c
201 between 0.9 and 1 T (Figure 2a-2). However, IRM component analysis indicates that two
202 coercivity components can be identified, a dominant component with median acquisition
203 field (B ) of 600~630 mT that contributes 90% of the IRM and a small component
H1/2
204 (10%) with median acquisition field (B ) of ~100 mT (Figure 2a-3).
L1/2
205 For Group II samples (~14 specimens / 2 sites), two NRM components are identified
206 from TD analysis (Figure 2b-1). Component A (Comp A) is isolated below 670 (cid:113)C, and
207 accounts for 70-80% of the initial NRM intensity. It is northwest-directed with a steep
208 positive inclination, close to the direction of Group I samples, which is distinct from the
209 present-day geomagnetic field direction. A second component, designated as component
210 B (Comp B), is resolved between 670 and 690 (cid:113)C with 5 demagnetization steps and is
211 directed to the northwest with a shallow negative inclination in geographic coordinates.
212 M-T curves decay gradually to 670 (cid:113)C and then drop to zero abruptly at ~685 (cid:113)C, which
213 is consistent with the NRM TD results (Figure 2b-4). Bulk B for a representative sample
c
214 is ~398 mT from an unsaturated hysteresis loop (Figure 2b-2), with two coercivity
215 components identified from IRM analysis with B of 700~710 mT (i.e. higher than that
H1/2
216 of Group I) and B of ~200 mT (Figure 2b-3) (higher than that of Group I).
L1/2
217 Group III samples (~33 specimens / 4 sites) also have two magnetic components,
218 where Comp A dominates up to 670 (cid:113)C with a northeast direction and steep
219 downward-directed inclination in situ, and Comp B is resolved from 670 to 690 (cid:113)C with a
9

### page_41
220 northeast direction and shallow positive inclination (Figure 2c-1). M-T curves of Group
221 III samples are similar to those of Group II samples, with magnetic ordering temperatures
222 of ~685 (cid:113)C (Figure 2c-4). The bulk B for representative Group III samples is ~230 mT
c
223 (Figure 2c-2), and IRM acquisition curves can be fitted with two components with B
H1/2
224 of ~430 mT and B of ~60-65 mT (Figure 2c-3), both lower than the equivalent
L1/2
225 fractions in Groups I and II.
226 The model of Jiang et al. (2015) was used to analyze NRM TD curves for the three
227 sample groups to assess whether the NRM is a CRM or a DRM. Curves for Group I
228 samples have a concave shape and decay to zero gradually, which is consistent with the
229 expectation for CRM behaviour (Figure 3a). Samples from the other two groups yield
230 curves with similar shapes to those expected for a DRM, with abrupt decreases to zero at
231 ~670-690 (cid:113)C (Figure 3b). Based on TD and rock magnetic results, Group I samples are
232 interpreted to have been completely remagnetized by a CRM, while samples from the
233 other two groups are partially remagnetized and record a mixture of a CRM and a DRM.
234
235 3.2 Rock magnetic monitoring of CD-TD behaviour of red bed samples
236 To monitor the CD-TD behaviour of different coercivity components, stepwise
237 CD-TD treatment of a three-component IRM was carried out on a series of sister
238 specimens. Before CD treatment, the medium (50-500 mT) and hard (>500 mT)
239 components are dominant (Figure 4a-c). During stepwise CD treatment, the IRM
240 decreases sharply to become constant after six steps for Group I samples (Figure 4a),
241 while for the other two sample groups, the IRM is more resistant to CD treatment and
242 ceases to decrease further after 12 and 8 steps, respectively (Figure 4b, c). During
243 subsequent TD treatment, the medium coercivity component is dominant. The soft
244 component for all samples is unblocked below ~600 (cid:113)C, while the medium and hard
10

### page_42
245 components are completely unblocked at ~680 (cid:113)C. In addition, a weak Verwey transition
246 is detected in low-temperature ZFC curves (Figure 5a-c), which indicates that magnetite
247 occurs in the samples. For samples after 14-step CD treatment, an obvious Verwey
248 transition is observed but the IRM intensity has decreased to 10% of that before CD
249 treatment (Figure 5d-f). We infer that the expression due to magnetite may be concealed
250 by massive amounts of hematite in the non-leached samples. After CD treatment,
251 hematite pigment is dissolved, so magnetite can be detected more easily with magnetic
252 methods, which supports the notion that pigmentary hematite is dissolved preferentially,
253 and that detrital magnetite is more difficult to dissolve (Hu et al., 2013). Therefore, we
254 conclude that magnetite is responsible for the soft IRM component and that hematite is
255 responsible for the latter two components.
256 IRM acquisition curves after each CD leaching step were determined for 52 samples.
257 Two coercivity components can be identified from the IRM acquisition curves, a
258 dominant component with high coercivity of B and a soft component with coercivity
H1/2
259 of B (representative examples are shown in Figure 4d-f and Table 2). B and B
L1/2 H1/2 L1/2
260 decrease during progressive CD treatment for samples from the three identified groups.
261 For Group I samples (13 specimens), B decreases from ~800 mT to ~100 mT, while
H1/2
262 B decreases from ~80 mT to ~20 mT (Figure 4d), which leads to a decreasing bulk B .
L1/2 cr
263 It also suggests that both the “hard” and “soft” components are attacked by the acid, so
264 that coarse and fine particles become finer or are dissolved completely. For the other two
265 sample groups, II and III, coercivity variations during CD treatment are not as marked as
266 for Group I samples (Figure 4d-f). For Group II samples (6 specimens), B decreases
H1/2
267 from ~700 to ~400 mT, and B decreases from ~200 to ~40 mT (Figure 4e), while for
L1/2
268 Group III samples (33 specimens), B decreases from ~500 to ~200 mT, and B
H1/2 L1/2
269 decreases from ~60 to ~20 mT (Figure 4f). Based on the three-component IRM features
11

### page_43
270 (Figure 4a-c) and low temperature results (Figure 5), the low coercivity component with
271 B around 20 mT is interpreted to be magnetite.
L1/2
272
273 3.3 Comparison of chemical and thermal demagnetization results
274 For Group I samples, the primary NRM is difficult to identify with TD because it is
275 overprinted completely by a secondary CRM. However, a potentially meaningful ChRM
276 component can be identified from TD results for Groups II and III. Group I samples have
277 a brighter red colour and seem to be more weathered and pigmented than the others
278 which could explain the absence of a primary ChRM. This raises the question of whether
279 CD is more effective in isolating a ChRM in red beds, and whether it can resolve a
280 ChRM for Group I.
281 TD only (referred to as ‘direct TD’), CD, and combined CD-TD results are
282 summarized in Figure 6. Group I samples have a single linear trajectory in both CD and
283 TD; TD applied after completion of CD also reveals the same trajectory (Figure 6a). In
284 equal-area projections, demagnetization trajectories for TD and CD-TD overlap (Figure
285 6b). For stepwise CD and TD, about half of the NRM was demagnetized by CD (Figure
286 6c), with CD causing bleaching of the initially red samples (Figure 1c, d). For Group II
287 samples, direct TD and combined CD-TD yield contrasting results. A primary reversed
288 polarity direction was extracted from direct TD, while for the stepwise CD-TD protocol,
289 two components are identified. One component is similar to Comp A identified in the
290 direct TD protocol, while the direction for the latter is almost a vector combination of the
291 two components extracted from direct TD measurements (Figure 6d, e). Only 10% of the
292 NRM is left after CD (Figure 6f). For Group III samples, CD-TD reveals two
293 components, which are essentially parallel to the two components identified from direct
294 TD treatment (Figure 6g), with almost 85% of the NRM removed by CD.
12

### page_44
295
296 4. Discussion
297 4.1 Comparison of the effectiveness of thermal and chemical demagnetization
298 TD results allow identification of two components (Comps A and B) in samples
299 from Groups II and III (6 sites), while only Comp A can be distinguished in samples from
300 Group I (4 sites). Site mean directions (Fisher, 1953) are presented in Figure 7 and Table
301 1. The formation site-averaged direction for Comp A for all three groups is D = 355.1(cid:113), I
302 = 80.5(cid:113) (N= 10, (cid:78) = 35.9, (cid:68) = 7.3°) (Figure 7a). Directions for Comp B fall into two
95
303 groups, one with positive inclinations with a formation mean direction of D/I =
304 29.3(cid:113)/16.8(cid:113) (N = 4, (cid:78) = 35.7,(cid:68) = 10.9°), and the other with negative inclinations (D/I =
95
305 229.9(cid:113)/-12.8(cid:113), N = 2, (cid:78) = 45, (cid:68) = 10.1°), which is consistent with previous results from
95
306 this area (Opdyke et al., 1986; Su et al., 2005) (Figure 7b). Comp B directions pass a
307 reversals test at the 95% significance level (McFadden and McElhinny, 1990). Although
308 we cannot conduct a fold test because the sampled Huangmaqing Formation red beds are
309 monoclinal, the tilt test (Watson and Enkin, 1993; Enkin, 2003) for Comp B gives a
310 maximum grouping of directions at 144 percent unfolding (Figure S1). All of these
311 observations indicate that Comp B has a pre-folding origin. Thus, thermal
312 demagnetization is effective for analyzing partially remagnetized red beds with dispersed
313 unblocking temperature spectra. The direction obtained from CD treatment is similar to
314 that identified from TD for Comp A with steep downward-directed inclinations (Figure
315 7c); however, Comp B cannot be isolated from combined CD-TD treatment (Figure 7d).
316 Our results indicate that TD is more effective than CD, which raises the question of why
317 CD is less effective in thesesamples.
318 Red bed NRMs are generally a composite of a DRM and CRM, where the former
319 is often thought to be carried by rather coarse detrital magnetic minerals (i.e., hematite or
13

### page_45
320 magnetite), while the latter is recorded by fine-grained hematite pigment (e.g., Collinson,
321 1974; Larson and Walker, 1975; McClelland, 1996; Iosifidi et al., 2010). Fine-grained
322 hematite pigment is expected to be more soluble than the coarser detrital hematite
323 particles. HCl leaches all iron oxides, and removes the most soluble grains first leaving
324 less soluble grains behind (Burek, 1969; Park, 1970; Henry, 1979; Tauxe et al., 1980).
325 For example, fine-grained hematite cement has a high propensity to dissolve and,
326 therefore, dissolves readily, leaving behind partially dissolved specularite (Henry, 1979;
327 Cornell and Giovanoli, 1993). This allows identification of the magnetization component
328 carried by detrital specularite. Therefore, CD could be useful when dealing with
329 sediments with multicomponent magnetizations within a single sample, such as a DRM
330 and CRM. However, if the solubility spectra of hematite cement and specularite overlap
331 in some unknown fashion, simple vector subtraction cannot be used to identify the
332 respective components.
333 IRM unmixing analysis indicates that low- (~100-200 mT) and high-coercivity
334 (~500-700 mT) components can be separated (Figure 2), which may reflect different
335 particle size distributions of hematite based on the positive relationship of particle size
336 and coercivity. During acid leaching, the coercivities of the two components decrease
337 simultaneously (Figure 4e-f), which indicates a particle size decrease for both
338 components (Hartstra, 1982; Dekkers and Linssen, 1989). Thus, fine and coarse particles
339 both dissolve during this process, so that the paleomagnetic direction identified with CD
340 is in principle the vector sum of the two components identified from direct TD (Figure 6d,
341 g). Tauxe et al. (1980) conducted chemical leaching on Siwalik red beds in which the
342 dominant magnetic carrier is hematite and found that the bulk remanent coercivity
343 decreases after acid leaching, so they deduced that hematite pigment is magnetically
344 harder than specularite because they assumed that only pigment was dissolved. Our
14

### page_46
345 results provide a reasonable explanation for the decreased bulk coercivity, where both
346 low and high coercivity components dissolve during acid leaching (Figure 4d-f).
347 Hematite is presumably present in various forms with diverse origins (Walker et al.,
348 1981), which refines the commonly held view that hematite in red beds can be divided
349 into just two groups: pigment and detrital specularite. Authigenic hematite occurs not
350 only as pigment, but also as microcrystalline, polycrystalline, and monocrystalline grains
351 with sizes in the micrometer range (Walker et al., 1981), which will not dissolve as
352 readily as pigment. Therefore, CD is not so effective in removing secondary hematite
353 with a wide particle size distribution. However, for red bed samples with distinct particle
354 size distributions, such as pigment and specularite, CD could provide meaningful results
355 (Henry, 1979; Tan et al., 2007).
356
357 4.2 Remagnetization mechanism for the steep magnetization component
358 A strong secondary vertically-directed magnetization component is often observed
359 in Triassic samples from South China (Figure 8), including the studied Huangmaqing
360 Formation in Nanjing (Kent et al., 1986, 1987; Opdyke et al., 1986; Su et al., 2005), the
361 Anshun and Huaxi Formations in Guizhou province (Huang and Opdyke, 1996, 2015)
362 and Hubei province (Huang and Opdyke, 1997, 2000), the Badong Formation in the
363 border area between Sichuan, Hubei and Hunan provinces (Huang and Opdyke, 1991,
364 1992), and the Tongtoujian Formation in Anhui province (Gilder et al., 1999; Su et al.,
365 2005). However, the origin of this component is unclear (Opdyke et al., 1986). Previous
366 studies have proposed that it might represent a multicomponent magnetization that yields
367 a vertical resultant, with overprinting in a post-folding steeply inclined magnetic field
368 (Opdyke et al., 1986) that might be related to late Mesozoic Yanshanian orogenic activity
369 in these parts of South China (Kent et al., 1987; Wang and van der Voo, 1993), which led
15

### page_47
370 to substantial intracontinental tectonic rotations.
371 Red bed remagnetization usually results from secondary hematite formation via
372 crystallization from solution or by mineral alteration. For the former mechanism, the
373 CRM can record faithfully the magnetic field direction if it is a single-stage growth
374 process (Stokking and Tauxe, 1987, 1990a; Jiang et al., 2015), while the magnetization
375 direction for the latter mechanism will be controlled by both the remanence of the parent
376 mineral(s) and the ambient magnetic field direction (Heider and Dunlop, 1987; Stokking
377 and Tauxe, 1990b; Madsen et al., 2002). In our experiments, only hematite components
378 with unblocking temperatures between ~650(cid:113)C and 685(cid:113)C are interpreted as a ChRM in
379 the direct TD results (Figure 2). However, based on CD-TD treatment of a
380 three-component IRM, magnetite is detected in the low-coercivity component with a
381 Curie temperature below 600 (cid:113)C after CD (Figure 4a-c); this component is not observed
382 in direct TD results for a three-component IRM because hematite is so dominant (Su et
383 al., 2005). A Verwey transition is also more evidentin low-temperature ZFC curves for
384 samples after CD treatment (Figure 5). We deduce that this magnetite is concealed by its
385 small concentration with respect to the large hematite pigment concentration, which
386 precludes its detection by direct TD. Magnetite may also be a parent mineral for
387 secondary hematite.
388 Paleomagnetic poles for Comp B (Figure 9) cluster alongside those from previous
389 studies and close to the position of Triassic paleomagnetic poles, which further indicates
390 that Comp B is a primary NRM component. However, the paleomagnetic pole for Comp
391 A lies far from the apparent polar wander path of the South China Block (Figure 9),
392 which suggests that the recording of Comp A was controlled not only by the ambient
393 paleomagnetic field, but also by additional factors. Parent magnetic particles can control
394 second-generation particles through magnetostatistic or exchange interactions (Stokking
16

### page_48
395 and Tauxe, 1990b), which leads to a CRM with a direction intermediate between the
396 ambient magnetic field direction and the parent magnetic mineral direction (Heider and
397 Dunlop, 1987; Stokking and Tauxe, 1990b). Late Mesozoic Yanshanian orogenic activity
398 occurred pervasively in the South China Block. Previous studies indicate that the studied
399 Zijinshan hill formed during the Yanshanian orogeny (Xue et al., 1985; Ge, 1987); the
400 fluids produced could have caused conditions required for magnetite oxidation (Kent et
401 al., 1987). In addition, the stress field of an orogeny can play a role in CRM acquisition
402 by deviating it from the ambient field direction (Nagata, 1970; Gilder, 2007). Therefore,
403 we suggest that the direction of the secondary component was controlled by several
404 factors. Before the orogenic activity and diagenesis, the paleomagnetic field is inferred to
405 have been recorded faithfully by Comp B, which is carried by detrital magnetite and
406 hematite. However, during or after tectonic activity, the accompanying temperature
407 increase would have promoted magnetite oxidation. During this process, a tectonically
408 rotated parent remanence carried by magnetite with the influence of a contemporaneous
409 ambient geomagnetic field and stress field generated by tectonic activity are argued to
410 have produced the steep downward-directed magnetization in the studied samples. We
411 suggest that this is why a steep magnetization component is commonly observed in
412 different areas of the South China Block.
413
414 5. Conclusions
415 Based on systematic thermal and chemical demagnetization, and rock magnetic
416 analysis, thermal demagnetization is more effective in isolating an apparently primary
417 magnetization than chemical demagnetization in red beds from South China. Two
418 remanence components carried by secondary and primary hematite are isolated with
419 thermal demagnetization, where the latter records a paleomagnetic direction that is
17

### page_49
420 consistent with published results. However, chemical demagnetization fails to extract a
421 ChRM direction from the remagnetized component due to simultaneous dissolution of
422 both fine and coarser hematite particles.
423 The presence of magnetite provides clues to the remagnetization mechanism in these
424 samples. The CRM carried by secondary hematite is interpreted to have been generated
425 by magnetite oxidation during tectonic activity. Therefore, the secondary magnetization
426 with steep inclination,which is observed commonly in Triassic samples from different
427 areas of the South China Block, is interpreted to have been influenced by a combination
428 of the remanence carried by parent magnetite, the orogenic stress field, and the
429 contemporaneous geomagnetic field direction during deformation. Our results shed new
430 light on interpretation of paleomagnetic results from remagnetized red beds and are
431 significant for tectonic studies of southern China.
